notes.subject: ENGLISH
notes.title: Parts of Speech
notes.summary: Every word belongs to a part of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, or interjection.
key_ideas: Nouns name people, places, things or ideas.
Verbs show action or state.
Adjectives describe nouns; adverbs describe verbs, adjectives or other adverbs.

sections.heading: Nouns and pronouns
sections.explanation: Common noun: city. Proper noun: Asmara. Pronouns replace nouns: he, she, it, they, someone.

sections.heading: Verbs
sections.explanation: Action: run, write. Linking: is, seem. Helping: have, will, can. Agree with the subject: She writes / They write.

sections.heading: Adjectives and adverbs
sections.explanation: Adjective: a bright student. Adverb: she studies carefully. Many adverbs end in -ly, but not all (fast, well).

sections.heading: Prepositions and conjunctions
sections.explanation: Preposition: in, on, at, between. Conjunction: and, but, because, although.

examples.title: Identify
examples.problem: In “The quick fox jumps,” label each word.

exercises.explanation: It describes how something is done.

notes.subject: ENGLISH
notes.title: Sentence Structure and Tenses
notes.summary: A complete sentence needs a subject and a predicate. Verb tense shows time: present, past, future — with simple, continuous and perfect forms.
key_ideas: Subject–verb agreement is required.
Tense must match the time meaning.
Avoid mixing tenses without reason.

sections.heading: Simple tenses
sections.explanation: Present: She studies. Past: She studied. Future: She will study.

sections.heading: Continuous
sections.explanation: Present continuous: She is studying. Past continuous: She was studying when I called.

sections.heading: Perfect
sections.explanation: Present perfect: She has studied this unit. Past perfect: She had studied before the test.

sections.heading: Agreement
sections.explanation: He walks / They walk. Everyone is ready (singular).

exercises.prompt: Correct: He go to market every day.
exercises.answer: He goes to market every day.

notes.subject: ENGLISH
notes.title: Active and Passive Voice
notes.summary: Active: subject does the action. Passive: subject receives the action. Form passive with be + past participle.
key_ideas: Active: The student wrote the essay.
Passive: The essay was written by the student.
Use passive when the doer is unknown or less important.

sections.heading: Forming the passive
sections.explanation: Object of active becomes subject of passive. Verb: be + past participle. Optional by-agent.

sections.heading: Tense in passive
sections.explanation: is written / was written / has been written / will be written.

sections.heading: When to use passive
sections.explanation: Science reports and news often focus on the result, not the doer.

examples.title: Convert
examples.solution: The scripts were marked by the teacher.

exercises.prompt: Passive: They will announce the results.

notes.subject: ENGLISH
notes.title: Clauses and Complex Sentences
notes.summary: Independent clauses stand alone. Dependent clauses need a main clause. Subordinating conjunctions build complex sentences.
key_ideas: because, although, if, when introduce dependent clauses.
Relative clauses use who, which, that.
A fragment is an incomplete thought.

sections.heading: Independent vs dependent
sections.explanation: She finished the exercise because she had studied.

sections.heading: Relative clauses
sections.explanation: The student who studied passed. The book that I borrowed is new.

sections.heading: Avoiding fragments
sections.explanation: “Because I was late.” needs a main clause: I apologized because I was late.

examples.title: Combine
examples.problem: He was tired. He continued studying. (although)
examples.solution: Although he was tired, he continued studying.

notes.subject: ENGLISH
notes.title: Conditionals
notes.summary: Zero, first, second and third conditionals express real or unreal situations.
key_ideas: Zero: facts.
First: real future.
Second: unreal present.
Third: unreal past.

sections.heading: Zero and first
sections.explanation: Zero: If + present, present. First: If + present, will + base verb.

sections.heading: Second and third
sections.explanation: Second: If + past, would + base. Third: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

sections.heading: Tips
sections.explanation: Formal second conditional: If I were you…

exercises.prompt: Fix: If he was taller, he will play.
exercises.answer: If he were taller, he would play.

notes.subject: ENGLISH
notes.title: Reported Speech
notes.summary: Reported speech restates what someone said. Tenses often shift back when the reporting verb is past.
key_ideas: Present → past with past reporting verb.
Pronouns and time words may change.
Commands: tell/ask + to-infinitive.

sections.heading: Statements
sections.explanation: “I am tired,” she said → She said she was tired.

sections.heading: Questions
sections.explanation: He asked if I was ready. She asked where I lived.

sections.heading: Commands
sections.explanation: “Sit down,” he said → He told me to sit down.

examples.title: Report
examples.solution: They said they would come the next day.

exercises.prompt: Report: “Where is the library?” he asked.
exercises.answer: He asked where the library was.

notes.subject: ENGLISH
notes.title: Punctuation and Conciseness
notes.summary: Punctuation clarifies meaning. Concise writing removes empty words without losing meaning.
key_ideas: Do not join two independent clauses with only a comma.
Apostrophes mark possession or contractions, not plurals.
Parallel lists use the same form.

sections.heading: Commas and splices
sections.explanation: Wrong: She studied, she passed. Right: She studied, and she passed.

sections.heading: Apostrophes
sections.explanation: Student’s / students’. It’s = it is. Its = possession.

sections.heading: Conciseness
sections.explanation: Due to the fact that → Because. In order to → to.

examples.title: Fix
examples.problem: The girls book is on the table.
examples.solution: The girl’s book is on the table.

exercises.answer: He ran, and he won. / He ran; he won.
exercises.explanation: Need a conjunction or stronger punctuation.

notes.subject: ENGLISH
notes.title: Essay and Argument Structure
notes.summary: Introduction with thesis, body with evidence, conclusion. Arguments need claims, reasons and counterarguments.
key_ideas: One main idea per paragraph.
Use linking words: however, therefore, in addition.
Explain evidence; do not only list it.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.explanation: Hook + context + thesis stating your main claim.

sections.heading: Body paragraphs
sections.explanation: Topic sentence → explanation → evidence → link to thesis.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.explanation: Restate thesis, summarize points, final insight — no new argument.

examples.title: Thesis check
examples.solution: Too vague. Stronger: name the policy and reason.

exercises.prompt: What does a topic sentence do?
exercises.answer: States the main idea of the paragraph.
exercises.explanation: Everything in the paragraph supports it.

notes.subject: ENGLISH
notes.title: Common Grammar Errors
notes.summary: Agreement, articles, prepositions and run-ons cost marks. Use a short checklist before submitting.
key_ideas: One clear main verb per long sentence.
A/an non-specific; the specific.
Modifiers next to the word they describe.

sections.heading: Agreement and articles
sections.explanation: The list of items is long. A before consonant sounds; an before vowel sounds (an hour).

sections.heading: Prepositions
sections.explanation: Interested in, good at, depend on, arrive at/in.

sections.heading: Run-ons and modifiers
sections.explanation: Fix run-ons with period, semicolon or conjunction. Keep modifiers next to what they describe.

exercises.prompt: Correct: He is interested on biology.
